paper_sections.title: Cognitive and neural contributors to emotion regulation in aging

description.value: The study investigated cognitive and neural mechanisms of cognitive reappraisal in younger and older adults, including age effects and relationships between cognition and emotion-regulation-related brain activation.

spans.text: Here we compared the neural mechanisms of cognitive reappraisal in younger and older adults.

design.value: Younger and older adults completed psychometric testing and training in an emotion regulation task in one session and underwent fMRI scanning in a second session on a different day; the task used positive, negative, and neutral pictures with Experience and Reappraise conditions.

spans.text: Each person participated in two sessions on different days. The first session included a psychometric testing battery and training on our emotional reappraisal paradigm, and the second session involved fMRI scanning.
Older adults (range: 59–73 years) and younger adults (range: 19–33 years) participated in a cognitive reappraisal task during functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scanning.
All images were drawn from the International Affective Picture System ( Lang et al. , 2005 ).
Participants reported no history of neurological or psychiatric disorder and scored a 27 or above on the Mini-Mental State Examination ( Folstein, Folstein and McHugh, 1975 ).

task_description.value: Participants viewed positive, negative, or neutral photographic images and either experienced their emotions naturally or decreased their emotional response by reappraising the image.

spans.text: Each trial of this task began with a single photographic image that was negative, positive, or neutral in valence.

The image remained on screen by itself for 2 s, whereupon a 2-s verbal cue indicated whether the participant was to experience his emotions naturally (‘Experience’ condition) or to decrease his emotional response to the image (‘Reappraise’ condition).
The task was created using Psychtoolbox ( Brainard, 1997 ; Pelli, 1997 ).

We used two regression models for our analyses, one for condition effects and the other for interactions between regions.
All regressors were convolved with a double-gamma hemodynamic response function.

model_settings.value: The first model included five trial-type regressors, nuisance regressors for visual presentation and response periods, and whole-brain-corrected thresholds of voxel z > 2.3 and cluster P < 0.05. The second model used amygdala time courses, a regulation-condition boxcar, and PPI regressors.

spans.text: Our first model created five regressors of interest, one for each of the trial types (‘Experience-Positive, Experience-Negative, Experience-Neutral, Reappraise-Positive and Reappraise-Negative’).
